paper_title: SpecWM: Turning Verification into Refinement for Streaming World Models

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Recently, video world models have advanced interactive generation, with large models offering higher quality and smaller models enabling faster inference. Existing speculative methods combine their strengths through fast draft generation and selective target regeneration guided by rewards on decoded frames. However, verification covers only the external scorer's evaluation dimensions and adds decoding and scoring costs. Moreover, these scores provide no correction, requiring costly target regeneration for rejected drafts. To address these limitations, we propose Speculative World Model (SpecWM), a unified, training-free inference framework for streaming world models. It verifies draft chunks using the target's latent velocity field. Verification also yields a reusable correction; two thresholds select Accept, Refine, or Reject. Specifically, one-step refinement reuses it to improve perceptual quality, while three-step refinement strengthens camera following and trajectory consistency. These findings motivate transition-aware refinement. On WBench Navigation, SpecWM improves visual quality at 1.63$\times$ speedup over the target and raises NavScore from the draft's 75.99 to 85.63, achieving the best quality-speed-control trade-off. Additionally, our LongSpecBench shows sustained quality and control over long, multi-turn rollouts, while experiments on Hy-Nomas validate SpecWM across backbones and denoising budgets.

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: 1. Introduction Recently, video world models have advanced interactive generation, with large models offering higher quality and smaller models enabling faster inference. Existing speculative methods combine their strengths through fast draft generation and selective target regeneration guided by rewards on decoded frames. However, verification covers only the external scorers evaluation dimensions and adds decoding and scoring costs. Moreover, these scores provide no correction, requiring costly target regeneration for rejected drafts. To address these limitations, we propose Speculative World Model (SpecWM), unified, trainingfree inference framework for streaming world models. It verifies draft chunks using the targets latent velocity field. Verification also yields reusable correction; two thresholds select Accept, Refine, or Reject. Specifically, one-step refinement reuses it to improve perceptual quality, while three-step refinement strengthens camera following and trajectory consistency. These findings motivate transitionaware refinement. On WBench Navigation, SpecWM improves visual quality at 1.63 speedup over the target and raises NavScore from the drafts 75.99 to 85.63, achieving the best quality-speed-control trade-off. Additionally, our LongSpecBench shows sustained quality and control over long, multi-turn rollouts, while experiments on Hy-Nomas validate SpecWM across backbones and denoising budgets. Streaming world models enable users to explore generated environments that evolve in response to their actions [11, 17]. Such interaction requires high visual quality, accurate control following, and rapid responses to changing inputs. However, larger models offer stronger quality and control at substantial computational cost, whereas smaller models generate faster at the expense of visual quality and accuracy in following the controls (Fig. 1, right). Existing reward-based speculative methods combine these strengths through fast draft generation and selective target regeneration. Rewards computed on decoded draft frames determine which chunks to accept and which to regenerate with the target. Setting up this verifier requires choosing reward model, aggregating frame scores, and calibrating an acceptance threshold [16]. However, verification is limited to the attributes captured by the external scorer [44]. Decoding and scoring also add runtime costs per chunk. Moreover, these scores provide no direct refinement signal to improve the draft itself (Fig. 1, left). Consequently, every rejected draft requires computationally expensive regeneration by the target through its full sampling process, reducing the savings from fast draft generation. How can verification itself provide reusable correction to improve the trade-off among speed, visual quality, and control in speculative generation for streaming world models?

sections.title: Preprint
sections.content: 1 We propose Speculative World Model (SpecWM), unified, training-free inference framework that turns verification into refinement for streaming autoregressive (AR) world models. SpecWM replaces decoded-frame reward scoring with single final-stage evaluation of the targets latent velocity field v. This evaluation yields clean prediction under the same history and controls. Its difference from the draft provides verification score. Moreover, the same prediction supplies reusable correction. Based on this score, SpecWM uses two thresholds to select Accept, Refine, or Reject to allocate target computation across chunks. One-step refinement directly reuses the prediction from verification, without further target denoising. Three-step refinement starts at higher noise level and runs three consecutive target denoising steps. With verification fixed, our uniform-refinement experiments reveal complementary effects  (Table 1)  . One-step refinement improves imaging quality and perceptual preference over the draft, with limited improvement in navigation control. Three-step refinement strengthens camera following and trajectory consistency, but lowers perceptual preference and aesthetics relative to one step; imaging quality remains similar. Image diffusion studies link early denoising to coarse structure and later steps to fine detail [48]. Our results suggest similar distinction: final-stage correction improves appearance, while earlier intervention allows greater trajectory revision. These findings motivate transition-aware refinement. For chunks routed to Refine, SpecWM uses three steps at control change, two in the next chunk, and one thereafter. This schedule improves control near transitions while favoring perceptual quality and speed during continued motion. Throughout this schedule, verification remains fixed at one final-stage probe per draft chunk. Additionally, the draft generates the next chunk while the target verifies the current one, thereby reducing latency. Our main contributions are summarized as follows: SpecWM. We propose unified, training-free framework that turns verification into refinement. With transitionaware refinement, SpecWM achieves 1.63 generationloop speedup over Target-only on WBench Navigation [51], improving imaging quality and perceptual preference while maintaining target-level navigation control. LongSpecBench. We construct benchmark of long, multi-turn rollouts with revisits to jointly evaluate generation quality, speed, and sustained controllability. SpecWM leads the evaluated methods in world-model quality (WMQ) and quality-efficiency score (QES). Beyond model scale. SpecWM extends from modelscale to denoising-budget differences on Hy-Nomas [7], where draft and target share the same weights. It outperforms Draft-only and SDVG-style across four humanevaluated dimensions, achieving near-target preference at 1.33 generation-loop speedup over Target-only. 2. Related Work Autoregressive video generation and world models. Diffusion models [14], latent representations [37], and transformers [36] underpin video synthesis [1, 6, 12, 15, 47]. Building on this foundation, camera and motion conditioning enable controllable generation [13, 43], while flexible temporal conditioning incorporates generation history [4, 41]. For streaming generation, causal distillation reduces latency [50, 52], and training on self-generated histories addresses the training-inference mismatch [18]. Longer rollouts further require managing accumulated errors through long-video tuning, cache refreshes, and rolling denoising [26, 46]. These developments support interactive world models that respond to user actions [2, 7, 11, 17]. Evaluation likewise extends from video quality in VBench [19] to multi-turn interaction in WBench [51]. SpecWM addresses computation allocation during streaming inference to balance visual quality, speed, and control. Caching and efficient inference. Efficient samplers [28, 40], distillation [38, 49], and consistency models [42] reduce denoising steps. Beyond reducing steps, caching exploits redundancy in features, attention, and guidance [29, 30]. Adaptive reuse responds to estimated output changes or chunk-level variation [25, 32]. For world models, selective token recomputation [10] and history-guided caching with residual correction [35] address reuse across evolving content. System optimizations combine caching with sparse attention, quantization, and kernel fusion [22]. These approaches lower the cost of running generator by reusing internal computations or reducing sampling steps. SpecWM instead allocates computation according to the draft chunks discrepancy from the target. Accept, Refine, and Reject provide different levels of target intervention. This allocation applies to pairings with different model scales or denoising budgets, including shared-weight configurations. Speculative verification and refinement. Speculative decoding combines draft proposals with target verification [5, 20]; feature prediction and multiple decoding heads improve proposal generation [3, 21]. DSpark uses confidence and serving load to schedule token verification [8]. In video generation, SDVG uses ImageReward [44] on decoded draft frames to select acceptance or target regeneration [16]. However, this verifier incurs decoding and scoring costs, and its coverage depends on the external scorer. Moreover, the scores guide selection without supplying direct correction. Separately, other methods allocate computation within one generator: Speculative Forcing freezes converged tokens [9], while Surprise Forcing skips steps according to chunk difficulty [39]. SpecWM instead verifies draft chunks using the targets latent velocity prediction. The resulting clean estimate can correct the draft, adding refinement between acceptance and full regeneration. 2 Figure 2. SpecWM overview. These counts describe target denoising work; draft generation and cache updates add separate costs. Sampling and evaluation details appear in the supplementary material. Human preference and efficiency. SpecWM achieves near-target human preference at 1.33 generation-loop speedup  (Fig. 6)  . Against Target-only, ties dominate each dimension, with comparable win and loss rates. SpecWM also records positive win-loss margins against Draft-only and SDVG-style across all four dimensions. Compared with SDVG-style, higher preference in camera control and spatial memory accompanies faster generation. Together, relative preference scores and speedups summarize SpecWMs balance between human preference and efficiency. Across backbones and sampling budgets. Together with LingBot, these results validate SpecWM across backbones and pairing strategies. Specifically, LingBot uses different model scales, whereas Hy-Nomas varies the sampling budget within one network. Finer denoising steps provide corrections without increasing model capacity. SpecWM accelerates generation even with identical model weights. Native sampling budgets offer another way to form draft-target pairs without training separate draft model. 6. The targets latent velocity prediction supplies both verification signal and reusable correction, reducing reliance on costly regeneration. Our experiments reveal complementary benefits of short and long refinements for perceptual quality and trajectory control. Transition-aware refinement combines these benefits, achieving the best overall quality-speed-control tradeoff among the evaluated methods on WBench Navigation and our LongSpecBench. Hy-Nomas further demonstrates effective pairing through different denoising budgets with shared weights. Together, these findings support verification-guided refinement across model-scale and sampling-budget differences. Future work will extend drafttarget pairing through cross-model latent alignment.
